title: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: F_2 = \phi(F_1), \phi : (x, y) \mapsto (x', y') a simple, symmetrical deformation of Cartesian coordinates

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We are dealing in this chapter with the forms of related organisms, in order to shew that the differences between them are as a general rule simple and symmetrical, and just such as might have been brought about by a slight and simple change in the system of forces to which the living and growing organism was exposed.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Theory of transformations”. Scope: related species within a zoological class (fishes, crustaceans, reptile and mammal skulls, etc.)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: F_2 = \phi(F_1), \phi : (x, y) \mapsto (x', y') a simple, symmetrical deformation of Cartesian coordinates

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern registration makes transformation complexity and residual error measurable, and public morphology covers many stated groups. Model comparison can decisively test the geometric rule, though it cannot by itself establish the proposed force mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Register homologous landmarks or surfaces for related species and compare simple symmetric Cartesian deformations with flexible and modular alternatives using held-out error and complexity penalties. Failure of simple models across sampled clades refutes the general rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
“Simple” and “general rule” require prespecified thresholds.

Homology and pose can affect registration.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.68
operationalizability: 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The theory of transformations is directly testable as a model-comparison problem on existing specimens. Open archives support that test for many pairs and fall short of a balanced sample of every class he has in view. Results would show how often a simple map suffices in the sampled groups, which is a partial answer to a claim about the general rule.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For pairs of related species, compare held-out landmark error of a simple symmetrical map (affine, shear, or a low-order coordinate stretch) with a high-parameter warp. The claim is supported if the simple map is usually enough across fishes, crustaceans and skulls; frequent need for localized warps would refute 'as a general rule'.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Published scans over-represent a few clades relative to the full range of classes Thompson cites.

Simplicity is a continuous property, so the cutoff for a 'simple' map has to be chosen.
